lesson.title: Subnetting: Carving One Address Block Into Many Working Networks
lesson.summary: Subnetting extends an IPv4 address's network portion using a subnet mask, splitting one address block into smaller networks, each with its own usable host range computed directly from how many bits the mask sets aside.
lesson.body:
A single IPv4 network, whether it is a full class based block from the old addressing scheme or a block assigned under modern classless routing, is rarely the right size for how an organization actually wants to organize its devices. A subnet is a smaller network carved out of a larger IPv4 address block by extending how many of the 32 bits in the IPv4 address format are treated as identifying the network, rather than identifying an individual host on it, and the tool that records where that line falls is the subnet mask.

A subnet mask is itself a 32 bit value, written in the same dotted decimal notation as an address, where a run of 1 bits marks the network portion and the remaining 0 bits mark the host portion; a router or host finds an address's network by performing a bitwise AND between the address and the mask. The mask 255.255.255.0 sets the first 24 bits to 1, commonly written in CIDR shorthand as /24, leaving 8 bits for hosts. Those 8 host bits can represent 2 to the 8th power, or 256, combinations, but two are always reserved, the all zeros host bits identify the network itself and the all ones host bits are the subnet's broadcast address, leaving 254 usable host addresses on any ordinary /24 subnet, for example the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet running from 192.168.1.0 through 192.168.1.255, with 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.254 available to assign to devices.

Subnetting becomes genuinely useful when an organization needs to split one large block into several smaller, independently manageable networks, for instance separating a building's devices by floor or department. Borrowing additional bits from the host portion shrinks each resulting subnet but multiplies how many subnets exist: taking the same 192.168.1.0/24 block and extending the mask to /26, or 255.255.255.192, borrows 2 extra bits for the network portion, leaving only 6 host bits per subnet. That yields 2 to the 2nd power, or 4, subnets, each with 2 to the 6th power, or 64, total addresses and 62 usable host addresses after subtracting the network and broadcast addresses: 192.168.1.0/26, 192.168.1.64/26, 192.168.1.128/26, and 192.168.1.192/26.

Subnetting is what makes the fixed size blocks of the old IPv4 address class system, and the fixed size private IPv4 ranges defined in RFC 1918, practically usable at any scale an organization actually needs, rather than forcing every network to either waste addresses on a block far larger than necessary or run out of room entirely. It is also the mechanism that lets a single organization's IPv4 address space mirror its physical or organizational structure, isolating traffic and limiting the size of broadcast domains, all by choosing exactly where within those 32 bits the boundary between network and host is drawn, a decision that scales down to a home network with one /24 just as cleanly as it scales up to a campus network built from dozens of smaller subnets.
